analysis.one_liner: Bars new offshore oil and gas drilling leases next to any coastal state whose governor has banned such drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill to let coastal states block offshore drilling next to their waters never got a committee hearing or a vote and died when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to stop the Interior Department from issuing new drilling leases on federal waters that lie seaward of or next to a coastal state that has put a moratorium on drilling in its own waters. A governor's ban or a state law would therefore extend outward to the adjacent federal zone. The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities and the tourism and fishing businesses that depend on clean water, since drilling spills and platform construction next to their shores would be barred wherever the state has banned drilling. State governments gain a practical veto over federal drilling in waters adjacent to their coasts.

how_it_helps.text: When a coastal state has a moratorium on oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production in its own waters, the Interior Secretary could not issue a lease for such activities on submerged federal lands seaward of or adjacent to that state.
The ban would cover moratoria established by state statute or by order of the governor, giving a governor's declaration direct force over federal leasing decisions next door.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to new drilling areas near states with moratoria, and the federal Treasury would forgo some bonus bids, rents, and royalties from leases never issued. Energy production in those zones would not expand.

drawbacks.text: The bill hands governors a one-way veto over federal mineral leasing in waters beyond state jurisdiction, raising a federalism objection: a federal resource would be controlled by a single state official's order, with no balancing of national energy needs.
Blocking leases adjacent to moratorium states would reduce areas available for domestic offshore energy production and the federal royalty revenue those leases generate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For coastal states that have already chosen to ban drilling, the bill closes a real gap: drilling platforms just past the three-mile state line can affect the same beaches and fisheries as drilling inside it, and the bill makes the state's choice stick. The cost is forgone federal energy production and royalties in those zones and a precedent that one governor can veto development of federal waters. The bill was never amended or debated, so its broader fiscal and federalism effects were never weighed in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Barbara Boxer introduced the Coastal States Protection Act on May 14, 1998, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, the only committee action it ever received.
No markup, hearing, or floor vote appears in the action history, and the bill died at the end of the 105th Congress on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that hold or seek offshore drilling leases near moratorium states are better off, since the restriction never became law and federal leasing authority remained unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore drilling interests and the leasing status quo

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it on the Senate floor.

for.name: 8 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sen. Sarbanes, Sen. Robb, Sen. Lautenberg, Sen. Murray, and Sen. Graham.

against.name: Sen. Frank Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never brought it to a markup or vote; the record shows no committee action after referral.

against.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
against.role: Leaseholders and prospective bidders on Outer Continental Shelf tracts
against.what_they_did: Would have lost access to new federal drilling areas near moratorium states; industry groups have long opposed state-control measures over offshore leasing.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-chaired committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would bar new federal leases next to any state with a drilling moratorium, taking prospective tracts off the table. The public cost to coastal communities of drilling near their shores is exactly what the bill is designed to prevent, putting the industry's interest against the bill's beneficiaries.

These businesses depend on clean coastal water, and the bill would prevent drilling activity in federal waters directly adjacent to states that have banned it. Their gain comes from the same protection residents would get.

industries.industry: State and local governments of coastal states
industries.note: Governors and state legislatures would gain a statutory backstop making their drilling bans extend to adjacent federal waters, strengthening state control over their coastlines.
